title: Chardi kala as philosophy
hook: a settled optimism rooted in trust, not in circumstances

segments.voice: Yesterday, kaam, desire in its place: not killed and not crowned, but kept. Your line was desire in its place.

The email that says no. The test result. The car that won't start in the rain. A setback lands, and there's a phrase for how Sikhs try to meet it, a phrase that closes the Ardas, the standing prayer: chardi kala. Rising spirits. It showed up early on this path as hope that keeps getting up. Today it isn't a mood. It's a way of seeing the world, with roots that go down below the weather.
screen: `A SETBACK LANDS.` → `CHARDI KALA.` → `NOT A MOOD: A PHILOSOPHY.`

segments.voice: First, the line. The Ardas closes with these words: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhaane sarbat da bhala. In paraphrase: Nanak, with the Name, rising spirits; by your will, the good of all. Look at what chardi kala stands next to. Not good news. Not a lucky break. Naam, the Name. The rising is rooted. Second, roots, not circumstances. Ordinary cheer climbs and falls with the forecast. Chardi kala, as Sikhs describe it, rests on trust in the One, so it doesn't need the forecast to cooperate. A tree on a windy hill bends hard in a storm. It stays because of what's underground. Third, it doesn't pretend. Earlier in this stretch, the Gurus called pain a medicine, without ever pretending it isn't pain. Chardi kala doesn't deny the setback. It simply refuses to let the setback write the ending. Grief and rising spirits can sit in the same person on the same afternoon. Fourth, it faces outward. The line doesn't end with my spirits. It ends with sarbat da bhala, the good of all. In Sikh thought, rising spirits are meant to be shared. The one in chardi kala can be the one others lean on in a hard room: steady voice, warm tea, a joke at the right moment. Not because things are fine. Because the roots hold.
screen: `NAAM, THEN CHARDI KALA.` · `ROOTS, NOT THE FORECAST.` · `IT DOESN'T PRETEND.` · `RISING FOR THE GOOD OF ALL.` · then, large: `RISING, ROOTED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one setback from this week, small or not so small, and notice where it sits in your body. Breathe in and picture roots going down from where you sit, into ground the setback can't reach; breathe out and let the corners of your mouth lift a little, not because it's fine, but because you're still standing. If you pray, say the Ardas's closing words quietly: Nanak naam chardi kala.
Chardi kala as philosophy. Rising spirits, rooted in the Name and in trust, not in circumstances, and turned toward the good of all. Today's word.
Your line: rising, rooted. Bent by the storm, held by what's underground. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs close the Ardas with the words 'Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhaane sarbat da bhala', and speak of chardi kala as a settled, rising spirit grounded in trust in Waheguru rather than in how things are going.

chat.says: Chardi kala sounds like positive thinking. Is it just staying cheerful no matter what?
options: Not really. It's rising spirits rooted in the Name, and it can sit right beside grief.
Yes. It's keeping a good mood by refusing to think about what went wrong.
Mostly. It's the high spirits that come when life is going well for you.
